svg.text: VLA v540 — one clock tick (40 ms): a ConvDelta language model, 6 residual blocks of per-tick convs, each with a gated delta-rule memory per grid position

A · the whole model. --lm: text only · C 384 · 7×7 grid · 6 blocks · H 6 heads × d 32 per position · 25 Hz · 29.97M trainable · fixed state 2,145,073 values · input: the last 8 tokens on a learned map · trained 256 ticks at a time, half the documents unreset
each block: causal time conv (4 ticks) → 3 × (conv 3×3 + BN + ReLU) → delta-rule memory Δ with its state S
one block, zoomed in: pane B ▼
the sampled token → the next tick's input (training: the dataset's)
learned input map a[j, p]: tokens t … t−7 onto the grid
per-position gain G and bias P (learned)
causal depthwise conv over the last 4 ticks
Δ: gated delta-rule memory update and read
D flip-flop register, clocked every tick
(training: reset at half the document starts)
A third conv 3×3 + BatchNorm + ReLU in every block (--cd_convs 3), before the memory's projections: 18 spatial
convs in all instead of 12. Each adds 1.33M weights (29.97M trainable, from 22.01M) and about 9% more time per
tick in training. It reads no state, so the state is unchanged (2,145,073 values) and the windows still train in
parallel. The question it answers: is the per-tick spatial mixing, between the input and the memories, the
bottleneck? Same rows, window, lr and data as v538, so the two compare step for step.
As v538: the input grid is a learned map of the last 8 tokens (starting as concentric rings: t outermost,
t−3 at the centre), and in training half the document starts do not reset the state, a stress test for
perception discontinuities: the model must let go of the previous document's memories itself.
Otherwise as v536: --lm, 6 ConvDelta blocks, AdamW (β 0.9, 0.95), lr warmed to 0.001, 32 × 256 tokens per update.

x: 384×7×7 per tick · H = 6 heads of d = 32 at each of the 49 positions · every operation is per position except the 3×3 convs
S ← α · S (I − β k kᵀ) + β v kᵀ
erase what k pointed at, write v there,
no weights of its own: S is state (fast weights),
learned only through the 1×1 convs feeding it
Training: everything before Δ runs on all
256 ticks of a window (32 rows) at once.
q, k, v, β, α for the window go to a
chunked scan (the WY form of the delta
rule, Yang et al. 2024), giving every S q
exactly. The state carries on between
windows; the gradient stops at a window's start.
Chip: one tick at a time. Per block it
holds S and the 3-tick FIFO, and does
Same results as training, by construction.
L2: q, k scaled to unit length per head (keeps S bounded)
causal depthwise conv over time, 4 taps
gates: β = σ(·), α = exp(−2 exp(λ) σ(·)), λ per head
D flip-flop register, clocked every tick
(S and the FIFO; training: reset at half the document starts)
